You'll build the technical models and interference analysis, from first principles, that decide who gets access to spectrum and how. That analysis becomes the regulatory rules and informs the advice ministers act on. This isn't a licensing or admin role. It's the engineering foundation underneath national spectrum policy, and it demands genuine intellectual depth: multi-technology, first-principles thinking, not simply following established rules. A recent piece of work from this team freed up satellite spectrum that lifted broadband capacity for rural New Zealand. That's the scale of outcome this role can produce. As an Australian citizen, you can live and work in New Zealand without a visa, and land in Wellington: a small, vibrant capital with a good vibe, a lower cost of living, and a shorter commute than anywhere you've worked before. The work is complex requiring technical analysis that shapes national policy and earns you a seat at the table at the United Nations and access to government. Few roles offer that combination of intellectual weight and quality of life. This one does. Why is this role different? In a large telco or regulator, this kind of work gets split into narrow, siloed roles.
